questions.q: What does `scipy.integrate.quad` return, and why is that useful?
options: Only the integral's value, with no indication of accuracy
A tuple of the estimated integral value and an estimate of the absolute error, which is worth checking when precision matters
A random sample from the integrand's distribution
The derivative of the function at the midpoint of the interval
questions.explain: quad returns both the estimated value of the definite integral and an error estimate, so you can judge whether the computed precision is good enough for the task at hand rather than assuming the first number is exact.

questions.q: Why is `brentq` described as the 'right default' for root-finding when solving for bond yield-to-maturity?
options: It requires no information about the function other than a single starting guess
It needs a bracketing interval where the function changes sign, and is then guaranteed to converge, combining bisection's reliability with faster convergence
It only works on linear functions
It automatically finds the global minimum of any function
questions.explain: brentq requires a bracket [a, b] where the target function (e.g. model price minus target price) has opposite signs at the endpoints, and is then guaranteed to converge to a root within that bracket — a safety guarantee newton doesn't offer.

questions.q: What is a key risk when using `optimize.newton` to solve for implied volatility compared to using `brentq`?
options: newton always converges faster but gives a less precise answer
newton has no bracket to stay within, so a bad starting guess can cause it to fail to converge or converge to an unintended root
newton cannot be used with the Black-Scholes formula at all
newton requires the function to be integrated first
questions.explain: Because newton (Newton-Raphson/secant) only uses a starting guess and no bracket, a poor initial guess can cause divergence or convergence to the wrong root — a risk brentq avoids by requiring a sign-changing bracket.

questions.q: When should you reach for `scipy.optimize.root` instead of `brentq` or `newton`?
options: When solving a system of several coupled nonlinear equations in several unknowns, rather than one equation in one unknown
Only when the function has no real roots
Whenever integrating a function over an interval
root is a direct, interchangeable replacement for brentq with identical requirements
questions.explain: root is designed for systems of equations with multiple unknowns that are solved jointly (e.g. two coupled model parameters against two market observables), unlike brentq and newton, which solve one equation in one variable.

questions.q: What makes solving for bond yield-to-maturity and option implied volatility fundamentally the 'same kind' of problem?
options: Both require Monte Carlo simulation to solve
Both are root-finding problems: finding the input (yield or volatility) that makes a pricing function's output match an observed market price
Both can only be solved using matrix inversion
Neither problem actually requires any numerical method — both have closed-form solutions
questions.explain: In both cases, you're searching for an unknown input value that makes a pricing formula's output equal an observed price — the defining shape of a root-finding problem, even though the specific formulas (bond discounting vs. Black-Scholes) differ.
